questions.q: What are the three layers every enterprise metadata architecture is built from?
options: Extract, transform, load
Design, build, test
Plan, execute, review
Harvest, store, serve
questions.explain: Any specific tool is really just one implementation of the harvesting, storage, and serving layers.

questions.q: What is the main architectural drawback of pull-based (crawling) metadata harvesting?
options: It requires every source system to actively cooperate
It only works for business glossary tools
Metadata can go stale between scheduled scans
It cannot be used with cloud data sources
questions.explain: A pull/crawl architecture only knows the current state when it runs its next scheduled scan — a change can sit uncaptured until then.

questions.q: Why do many metadata and catalog platforms store metadata as a graph underneath their UI?
options: Because questions like "what's downstream of this column" are graph-traversal questions, not simple lookups
Because regulations require metadata to be stored as a graph
Because graph databases are always faster than search indexes
Because graphs require less storage than relational tables
questions.explain: Relationships between assets, terms, and people are the whole point — and relationship-heavy questions are exactly what a graph structure is built to answer.

questions.q: In a federated metadata architecture, how is metadata typically organized?
options: Multiple stores, often per domain or platform, connected by APIs that sync or query across them
A single spreadsheet shared across the whole organization
No storage at all — metadata is regenerated on every query
One single store that every team is required to use
questions.explain: Federated architecture spreads metadata across multiple stores rather than one central repository, connected by integration rather than consolidation.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how does the metadata architecture decision relate to the operating model decision from Chapter 2?
options: They are unrelated and never influence each other
The operating model is about who owns what; the metadata architecture is about where the data technically lives — they usually mirror each other but don't have to
They are always identical decisions made by the same person
The metadata architecture decision always overrides the operating model
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a federated operating model can still choose a centralized store, and vice versa — the two decisions are related but separate.
